title: 23,000 Indian Sailors Trapped in Gulf's War Zone
excerpt: India's Directorate General of Shipping sets up 24x7 monitoring as the Strait of Hormuz crisis enters its third month with no end in sight.
body:
An estimated 23,000 Indian seafarers are now caught inside one of the world's most dangerous stretches of water, as the closure of the Strait of Hormuz — triggered by the US-Israel war on Iran that began February 28 — drags into its third month with no clear resolution.

**What is happening at sea:**
India's Directorate General of Shipping (DGS) confirmed that approximately 23,000 Indian seafarers are currently serving aboard vessels operating in the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, and adjoining waters. Among them, 768 crew members on 28 Indian-flagged ships remain stranded after ship movements were suspended due to the security situation. The UAE alone hosts 12,830 Indian sailors, with thousands more spread across Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman, Iran, Kuwait, and Bahrain.

**What the crisis looks like up close:**
The UN's International Maritime Organization has called the situation 'unprecedented,' with around 20,000 seafarers across all nationalities trapped on roughly 1,500 vessels unable to exit the strait. Indian sailors have faced drone strikes, food and water shortages, and months of unpaid wages. On March 1, a 25-year-old Indian seafarer was killed by a projectile as he began his engine room shift. The Maritime Union of India has since announced an ex-gratia payment of Rs 12 lakh to families of member seafarers killed in the conflict. India's DGS has activated a round-the-clock communication centre, coordinating with the Ministry of External Affairs and Indian missions across the Gulf to track crew safety and facilitate repatriation — so far moving 215 sailors out of affected locations including Muscat and Bahrain.

**What to watch next:**
With US-Iran peace talks still inconclusive and Iran reportedly mining the strait, watch whether India's diplomatic back-channel with Tehran — which successfully secured passage for eight LPG tankers — can be scaled up to bring home the thousands of sailors still waiting.
